name: french beef and mushroom stew
instructions:
TWO VARIANTS. Both land on the same herb axis (rosemary + thyme + bay leaf), same acid (red wine — not cabernet), and the same umami-boost stack (tomato paste + worcestershire + cholula hot sauce). They're close to identical on ingredient adds — kept as separate variants because I anticipate future divergence (e.g., variant B leaning harder on the porcini + nutritional yeast umami stack; variant A staying purer to Julia's classical shape).

=== VARIANT A — JULIA CHILD'S BOEUF BOURGUIGNON (WITH MY ADDITIONS) ===

Julia Child's canonical boeuf bourguignon from Mastering the Art of French Cooking, Vol. 1 — WITH my additions of rosemary, cholula hot sauce, and worcestershire sauce alongside her thyme + bay leaf. The rosemary is the biggest departure from Julia's original.

INGREDIENTS (per Julia, plus my adds):
- 6 oz chunk of bacon (rind removed and blanched separately; the bacon cut into lardons)
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 3 lb lean stewing beef (chuck), cut into 2-inch cubes
- 1 carrot, sliced
- 1 white onion, sliced (Julia calls for yellow; I use white per this cookbook's white-onion rule)
- salt + freshly ground black pepper
- 2 tbsp all-purpose flour
- 3 cups full-bodied young red wine (Burgundy / Chianti / Côtes-du-Rhône) — NOT cabernet, see notes
- 2-3 cups brown beef stock (enough to just cover)
- 1 tbsp tomato paste
- 2 cloves garlic, mashed
- 1/2 tsp thyme
- 1 bay leaf, crumbled
- blanched bacon rind (from the chunk of bacon)
- 18-24 pearl onions, braised separately in stock with a bouquet garni
- 1 lb fresh mushrooms, quartered, sautéed hard separately in butter
- MY ADDITIONS: fresh rosemary (in the braise), a few dashes of cholula hot sauce, a splash of worcestershire
- POTATOES ON THE SIDE (not in the stew) — mashed or roasted, served alongside. See POTATOES note.

PROCEDURE:
1. Simmer bacon rind + lardons in water for 10 min. Drain and pat dry.
2. Sauté lardons in olive oil in a heavy casserole; remove.
3. Brown the beef cubes in the same fat, in batches — real color, don't crowd. Remove.
4. Cook the sliced carrot + onion in the same fat until softened.
5. Return the beef + bacon to the casserole. Sprinkle with salt, pepper, and the 2 tbsp flour; toss to coat.
6. Uncovered in a 450°F oven for 4 min. Toss. Back in for 4 min more. (This browns the flour with the meat — Julia's specific step.) Reduce oven to 325°F.
7. Pour in wine + enough beef stock to just cover the meat. Stir in tomato paste, mashed garlic, thyme, bay leaf, and the blanched bacon rind. Add MY ADDITIONS: rosemary, worcestershire, cholula.
8. Bring to a simmer on the stovetop, cover, and braise in the 325°F oven for 3-4 hours (until fork-tender).
9. MEANWHILE: braise pearl onions (brown in butter, then finish in stock with a bouquet garni). Sauté quartered mushrooms hard in butter — don't crowd the pan.
10. Combine the braise + pearl onions + mushrooms at the end. Fish out the bay leaf and bacon rind. Taste; adjust salt, pepper, hot sauce.

No potatoes IN the stew for variant A (per Julia's canonical). Potatoes go on the side instead — mashed or roasted, alongside. See POTATOES note.

=== VARIANT B — VEGETARIAN (VEGAN MEAT + BUTTER BASE) ===

Structurally the current cookbook's beef-and-mushroom stew, built on ground vegan beef (Abbott's / soy beef crumbles) OR impossible/beyond formed into MEATBALLS (pre-baked, see notes). Fat base is BUTTER (main) — which makes this a VEGETARIAN dish, not vegan, even when the meat itself is vegan.

INGREDIENTS:
- BUTTER (main fat) + olive oil (supporting)
- ground vegan beef (Abbott's / soy beef crumbles) OR impossible/beyond meatballs (pre-baked; see IMPOSSIBLE/BEYOND note in the shared notes)
- white onions, coarse chopped
- carrots, coarse chopped
- garlic, mashed
- mushrooms (portabella / oyster / shittake — any or all), coarse chopped
- potatoes, coarse chopped ~1-inch chunks (LOAD-BEARING — see POTATOES ARE CRITICAL note)
- red wine (pinot noir / burgundy / syrah / malbec — NOT cabernet)
- bouillon or real vegetable/vegan-beef stock
- tomato paste
- fresh tomato, chopped (extra tomato flavor — see TOMATO note)
- rosemary, thyme, bay leaf (mandatory pair rosemary + bay leaf dominant; thyme supporting)
- worcestershire sauce (or vegan worcestershire if going fully vegan)
- cholula hot sauce
- red chili flakes
- nutritional yeast (secondary — part of the umami stack)
- porcini mushroom powder (secondary — reinforces mushroom depth)
- all-purpose flour (for the roux)
- salt + black pepper

PROCEDURE:
1. Sauté the mushrooms hard in butter first. This is the roux fond.
2. Whisk in flour for a roux (blond → light brown).
3. Add the coarse-chopped onions, carrots, garlic. DEEP SAUTÉ for real caramelization — don't rush this stage (see COARSE CHOP + DEEP SAUTÉ note).
4. Add wine + stock. Add potatoes, tomato paste, chopped fresh tomato, worcestershire, cholula, red chili flakes.
5. Add rosemary, thyme, bay leaf.
6. Add the vegan meat late in the braise: ground vegan beef stirred in, or pre-baked impossible/beyond meatballs nestled in.
7. Stir in nutritional yeast + porcini mushroom powder — small amounts, part of a broader stack.
8. Simmer until potatoes are tender and the stew has thickened. Fish out bay leaf.

See notes for shared rules (deep sauté, no fresh herbs, wine rules, fridge-aging behavior) and technique-specific callouts (pre-baking impossible meatballs, why potatoes are load-bearing here but not in variant A).

NOTE: a pure-vegetable variant was drafted here (celery root/turnips + no tomato + ginger/turmeric herbs + white wine) and rejected — didn't work well. That set of ideas moved to master-french-onion-vegetable-soup as its broader-vegetable variant, which is the right home for it.
notes:
French beef and mushroom stew — a bourguignon-shaped dish with two variants (see instructions for the full breakdown). Both share the shape: braised protein in red wine + tomato + herbs, with MUSHROOMS as a co-headliner alongside the meat.

- VARIANT A — Julia Child's canonical Boeuf Bourguignon (Mastering the Art of French Cooking, Vol. 1) with my adds: rosemary, cholula, worcestershire.
- VARIANT B — Vegetarian version: butter base + vegan meat (Abbott's / soy crumbles or pre-baked impossible/beyond meatballs), with potatoes as structural starch.

A VARIANT C (pure vegetable) was drafted and rejected — see the note in instructions. Those ideas moved to master-french-onion-vegetable-soup where they fit the register.

=== SHARED SHAPE — SOME KIND OF MEAT IS REQUIRED (REAL OR VEGAN); PURE VEGGIE DOESN'T WORK ===

This dish needs a protein slot filled with either REAL BEEF (variant A) or VEGAN MEAT (variant B — abbott's/soy crumbles or pre-baked impossible/beyond meatballs). Pure vegetable / mushroom-only doesn't work here — the dish loses its identity without a meat slot. If you want a pure-veggie french stew-adjacent dish, go to master-french-onion-vegetable-soup variant B; don't try to strip the meat out of this one.

MUSHROOMS AS CO-HEADLINER, NOT MEAT SUBSTITUTE: mushrooms aren't standing in for anything — they're the second headliner alongside the meat. Both slots need to be filled.

VEGETABLE BASE IS FIXED — CARROTS + MUSHROOM + ONION (BOTH VARIANTS), PLUS POTATOES (VARIANT B ONLY): the vegetable base is carrots, mushrooms, and onions across both variants, with potatoes ADDED IN VARIANT B ONLY (variant A serves potatoes on the side instead — see POTATOES note). Nothing beyond those four. If you want to add MORE vegetables (celery root, turnips, white beans, etc.), that's a signal you want a different dish — move to master-french-onion-vegetable-soup variant B, which is built for that broader-vegetable register. Don't extend this stew's vegetable base.

=== SHARED TECHNIQUE ===

COARSE CHOP + DEEP SAUTÉ (NO MIREPOIX): coarse-chop the onions, carrots, celery, and mushrooms into visible chunks — same rule as coq au vin. Rustic stew; you want visible pieces, not a dissolved mirepoix. But sauté HARD to get real caramelization before wine and stock go in. The deep-sauté / maillard phase does structural flavor work; rush it and the finished stew reads flat.

BALANCE FROM A MIX — NOT FROM ONE SAVORY HEADLINER: satisfying savory comes from a MIX of controlled amounts, not from cranking one dial. Small amounts of garlic, small tomato paste, controlled beef stock (or bouillon), controlled nutritional yeast, porcini mushroom powder. Each contributes some savory depth in a different register; overdoing any single one throws the balance off. Different from a dish like chile-colorado or american-chili where one flavor can lead — here the whole point is a layered supporting stack.

VARIANT B THICKENING: variant B starts with sauteed mushrooms in butter, then flour for a roux. Variant A uses Julia's flour-in-oven technique on the dredged meat instead (see instructions).

=== SHARED INGREDIENT RULES ===

STOCK — BEEF-FLAVORED IS BEST (BEEF > DARK VEGETABLE): both variants want beef-flavored stock or bouillon. Reach for BETTER THAN BOUILLON'S BEEF BASE if using a concentrated paste; real beef stock if you have it. Beef beats dark vegetable bouillon here — the beef stew register wants the beef flavor for real, not just savory-hearty depth. This is the OPPOSITE of what works in master-french-onion-vegetable-soup, where dark vegetable bouillon beats beef base.

WINE — NOT CABERNET: cabernet's tannins and fruit-forward jamminess dominate the sauce and push flavor toward a red-wine-reduction rather than a stew. A traditional burgundy or pinot noir works; a syrah or malbec is fine here (unlike coq au vin) — the beef and tomato paste can hold up to a bigger red. Just not cabernet.

NORTHERN PULL — WORCESTERSHIRE: worcestershire sauce rounds it out and pushes the flavor 'northern'. Without it the rosemary + bay + tomato combination can drift italian even with the potatoes.

RED CHILI FLAKES: a real ingredient here, not a topping. Pair particularly well with the tomato + worcestershire (or tamarind paste) axis — they activate the tang and amplify the depth. Stir into the simmer.

HOT SAUCE (CHOLULA): a splash alongside the red chili flakes for a second layer of heat + vinegar tang. Cholula (not tabasco), same preference as chicken-with-vinegar variant B.

NUTRITIONAL YEAST (SECONDARY): variant B specifically. Cheesy-adjacent savory depth. Small amount into the simmer — part of the broader stack, not solo umami.

PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER (SECONDARY): reinforces the fresh mushrooms without over-crowding the mushroom axis. Small amount stirred into the simmer.

SHARP WHITE ONIONS — NOT YELLOW OR RED.

GARLIC — NON-OPTIONAL.

CELERY AS RESCUE — WITH A MEDITERRANEAN COST: celery isn't primary but is an unusually useful correction. If you dumped in too much tomato paste, over-poured wine, or otherwise let one axis dominate, adding coarsely-chopped celery pulls flavors back toward center — its neutral savory-vegetal character absorbs excess tang. THE COST: celery drags the register toward mediterranean-vegetable-soup / minestrone territory — exactly the direction rosemary + bay + tomato is trying to escape. Use it to rescue a batch; a rescued stew reads slightly more italian and less french-classical. If using from the start (not as a fix), keep it modest — a stalk or two, coarse chop, not a full mirepoix.

HERBS / AROMATICS — ROSEMARY + BAY LEAF DOMINATE (BOTH VARIANTS): rosemary + bay leaf in large quantities are mandatory. The pair DOMINATES the herb axis. The wine + meat + mushrooms + carrots (+ potatoes in B) will be flat without them. Thyme welcome supporting; rosemary + bay stays dominant, not co-lead.

=== HARD RULES — WHAT NOT TO USE ===

NEVER FRESH HERBS OR FRESH GREENS — HARD RULE, LEARNED EARLY: FRESH HERBS (parsley, tarragon) and FRESH GREENS (spinach, mixed greens) are a hard 'never' here. Not 'use sparingly' or 'as a garnish' — actually leave them out.
- Fresh herbs (parsley, tarragon) → save for french chicken stews (french-chicken-soup, chicken-with-vinegar) where they carry the herb axis properly. This dish's herb axis is rosemary + bay leaf (dominant), thyme (supporting) — dried and cooked into the braise. Fresh finishing herbs fight that structure.
- Fresh greens → save for earthy italian tomato soups (italian-minestrone-soup family), or use as a side salad alongside this stew.

NO FENNEL BULB: doesn't work here. Save fennel bulb for master-french-onion-vegetable-soup or for ratatouille-shaped dishes without gravy elements.

NO PARSNIPS — TOO SWEET FOR THE BEEF VERSION: tomato + red wine + parsnips stacks up as a lot of fruity — three fruit-adjacent notes fighting each other. Reach for carrots (celery in a pinch) instead. Parsnips are a want-to-try over in master-french-onion-vegetable-soup variant B where the pure-vegetable register can absorb them.

=== VARIANT-SPECIFIC ===

MEAT — VARIANT A REAL BEEF; VARIANT B VEGAN MEAT (WITH BUTTER = VEGETARIAN):
- VARIANT A — REAL BEEF (CHUNKS): chuck (or similar stew-cut beef) cut into 2-inch cubes per Julia. Chunks carry the umami and texture the long braise needs; connective tissue breaks down over the cook to enrich the sauce.
- VARIANT B — GROUND VEGAN BEEF (ABBOTT'S / SOY BEEF CRUMBLES): the canonical variant B meat. Works better than chunky seitan (which stays rubbery and doesn't render). Ground vegan beef distributes through the dish and picks up the braise. NOTE: variant B uses BUTTER as the fat base (not bacon lardons like variant A), which makes the dish VEGETARIAN even when using vegan meat — not vegan.
- VARIANT B ALTERNATE — IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND BEEF AS MEATBALLS: usable in variant B when formed into MEATBALLS (see IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND note below on why meatballs, not crumbles, and the pre-bake step). Distinctly flavored, so use judgment.
- SOY CURLS: untested (see want_to_try). Curious whether they'd behave more like real beef chunks than seitan does.
Flavor in variant B is NOT derived from the meat itself; a good vegan beef bouillon or vegetable stock is doing the heavy lifting.

FAT BASE — VARIANT A: BACON LARDONS + OLIVE OIL; VARIANT B: BUTTER: real divergence, not a preference axis. Julia's variant A renders bacon lardons in olive oil (traditional bourguignon). Variant B uses BUTTER as the main fat with olive oil supporting — the butter enriches the mushroom sauté and gives the sauce body without needing bacon. The butter base is what makes variant B VEGETARIAN when using vegan meat (bacon would make it non-vegetarian). Don't add bacon to variant B; don't skip bacon in variant A (it's Julia's canonical).

POTATOES — VARIANT B GETS THEM IN THE STEW; VARIANT A GETS THEM ON THE SIDE:
- VARIANT B (VEGETARIAN): potatoes are load-bearing IN the stew. Coarse-chop ~1-inch chunks; add during the braise. They give the stew its starchy body and absorb the tomato-and-wine sauce properly.
- VARIANT A (JULIA'S BEEF): NO potatoes in the stew (per Julia's canonical). Serve potatoes ON THE SIDE instead — mashed or roasted alongside. The pearl-onion + separate-mushroom-sauté structure carries variant A without a starch component; the potato lives next to the plate, not in the pot.

WHY THE SPLIT: variant B's meat is less structural than real beef; the potato in the stew adds body and heft that vegan meat alone doesn't deliver. Variant A's real beef carries that weight on its own, so the potatoes are freed up to be a side rather than a filler. This also has fridge-aging implications (see FRIDGE-AGING note) — potatoes-in-stew fall apart over time, so keeping variant A's potatoes on the side is a bonus reason it lives longer than variant B in the fridge.

MAJOR DIFFERENTIATOR FROM COQ AU VIN: coq au vin has NO potatoes anywhere — pinot noir base would be dulled by the starch absorption if in the stew, and traditionally coq au vin is served with buttered egg noodles or crusty bread rather than potatoes.

IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND BEEF — COOK AS MEATBALLS, NOT CRUMBLES (VARIANT B ALTERNATE): if using impossible / beyond / similar extruded plant-based ground beef, form into MEATBALLS before adding to the stew. Don't break into crumbles — the extruded proteins recombine during baking, so crumbles turn back into a monolithic slab of pseudo-meat in the pot. Pre-formed meatballs hold their shape. This is unique to soy-based products; real ground beef and abbott's-style products don't behave this way.

PRE-BAKE THE MEATBALLS BEFORE ADDING TO THE STEW: bake formed impossible/beyond meatballs briefly at 350°F — NOT until fully cooked, just until they firm up on the outside so they hold shape and don't dissolve in the braise. The pre-bake gives them a slight surface set that survives the stew cook.

ROSEMARY IS RIGHT HERE, WRONG IN COQ AU VIN (SEE COQ-AU-VIN): coq au vin explicitly clashes rosemary — its pinot-noir-and-chicken register is too delicate and rosemary overpowers. This dish is the opposite: the wine is bigger, the meat is richer, and rosemary pulls it together. The two dishes are structurally opposed on this axis. Don't backport thyme + sage from coq au vin here (too subtle); don't backport rosemary to coq au vin (too aggressive).

=== FRIDGE-AGING BEHAVIOR — BEEF STEW'S MAIN ADVANTAGE ===

One of the big draws of beef stew is that it ages well in the fridge. Not all meat options preserve this:
- REAL BEEF (VARIANT A): fridge-friendly. Ages beautifully.
- GROUND VEGAN BEEF (ABBOTT'S / SOY BEEF CRUMBLES, VARIANT B): safer for fridge aging than impossible/beyond.
- IMPOSSIBLE / BEYOND BEEF: tastes good day-of, but causes the stew to AGE MORE POORLY in the fridge. Loses one of beef stew's main advantages.

VARIANT A WINS ON FRIDGE LIFE — TWO REASONS: variant A is inherently the longer-lived fridge stew. Two structural reasons stack:
1. REAL BEEF holds up (and improves) over multiple days in the fridge.
2. NO POTATOES IN THE STEW — variant A's potatoes live on the side (see POTATOES note). Potatoes-in-stew fall apart over time in the fridge — mushy survivors + broken-down starch that muddies the sauce. Variant A sidesteps this entirely.

Variant B has BOTH structural strikes against fridge life (impossible/beyond causes the sauce to age poorly; potatoes in the stew fall apart). Abbott's / soy crumbles helps with the first strike; nothing helps with the second short of serving variant B fresh.

If planning to eat across multiple days: reach for variant A. If cooking variant B, plan to eat it within a day or two.

(Earlier notes here suggested a 'just veggies' path as fridge-friendly — walked back. Pure veggie/mushroom-only doesn't work at all in this dish; see SHARED SHAPE note above.)

=== FORMAT & SERVING ===

DOESN'T WORK IN A POT PIE (UNLIKE THE CHICKEN VARIANT): this stew never works well in a pot pie, unlike julia child's master chicken stew (rosemary-chicken-pot-pie). Structural reasons:
- PEAS PAIR WITH CHICKEN, WHICH WORKS IN PIE FORM: chicken pot pie takes peas as a canonical addition, and peas hold up cleanly inside a pastry crust. Peas don't pair with beef + mushroom + tomato paste — the pie loses one of its structural components.
- CHICKEN SHREDS CLEANLY; VEGAN/IMPOSSIBLE BEEF (AND PROBABLY REAL BEEF) CLUMPS: shredded chicken distributes evenly through a pie filling. Ground vegan beef or impossible-beef meatballs clump into discrete chunks — reads wrong under a pastry lid.
- POTATOES ARE OPTIONAL IN CHICKEN POT PIE, LOAD-BEARING HERE: chicken variant doesn't need potatoes and often reads better without them. This stew's variant B has potatoes as a structural component — can't take them out for the pie format, and leaving them in creates gravy-absorption problems.

Net: format tradeoffs stack against the beef version. Keep this stew as a stew.

IF YOU WANT A HEARTY BEEF-FLAVORED / DARK PIE, LOOK ELSEWHERE:
- lentil-wellington (Nisha Vora's lentil-mushroom log in puff pastry) — built for the pie/pastry format, meat-analog umami stack (walnuts + mushrooms + miso + nutritional yeast + tomato paste) reads correct under pastry.
- atk-vegetable-pot-pie (STUB — unattempted): America's Test Kitchen's veggie pot pie with dark vegetable broth and turnips. Placeholder file exists; not yet captured or tested.

BEST PAIRING — HOMEMADE FRENCH ROLLS: the best pairing for this stew is homemade french rolls (see artisan-french-bread — bake as rolls rather than a loaf). The rolls do the sauce-sopping job a pastry lid would in a pot pie — but external to the dish, sidestepping the clumping/potato-absorption problems above. A crusty roll torn into the stew or used to soak the gravy on the plate is the intended eating experience.
why_i_like_this_recipe: It's the best hearty stew. It doesn't need to be in a pie (like julia child's chicken pie). It allows you to enjoy the components individually when they are on your plate (potato, carrot, mushroom and meat), but the broth is so good, you want to drink it anyway. It stays good in the fridge for days. It requires no blender or huge spice list.
